I was able to reproduce the problem, even though I am not sure exactly why there is a problem. A library that I was using to initialize some models when I was setting the state was creating a multiprocessing pool which in turn was creating an infinite loop of crashes. Minimal code to reproduce:
```
from multiprocessing import Pool
import streamlit as st

def add_one(x):
    return x+1

print([k for k in st.session_state])
if "state" not in st.session_state:
    print("Reloading")
    with Pool(8) as p:
        p.map(add_one, range(5))
    st.session_state["state"] = 1
```

This can be fixed by disabling the multiprocessing on the library end but I am wondering whats causing this on streamlit end and whether there is anything that can be done on streamlit side.

Part of the error is 
```
RuntimeError:
        An attempt has been made to start a new process before the
        current process has finished its bootstrapping phase.

        This probably means that you are not using fork to start your

```

This looks to me like a validation issue. If a key is provided, the value in that key should be used for validation instead of a default value defined by streamlit. This should just work:

```python
import streamlit as st
import datetime

min_date = datetime.date(2020,1,1)
max_date = datetime.date(2020,12,31)

if 'custom_date' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state['custom_date'] = min_date

st.date_input('Date', min_value=min_date, max_value=max_date, key='custom_date')
```

st.header("Workaround: Guard Expensive Work")
st.caption("✅ Prevents re-execution of expensive operations")

@st.dialog("Non-dismissible Dialog")
def working_dialog():
  # Initialize done flag on first run
  if "work_done" not in st.session_state:
      st.session_state.work_done = False

  # Only run expensive work if not already done
  if not st.session_state.work_done:
      st.write("Hang tight for a few seconds...")

      with st.empty():
          for x in range(1, 4):
              st.write(f"{x}...")
              sleep(1)

  st.success("All Done!")
  st.write("Click the button - expensive work won't re-run!")

  if st.button("Close", key="working_close"):
      # Clean up the flag
      st.session_state.work_done = False
      st.rerun()

+1, I was very excited to implement the new deferred download method and not make users click on two separate buttons, but without access to the variables nor session state - it quickly becomes useless for me.
The downloaded files content, in my use-cases entirely depends on the users input in other fields. I would even go as far as saying that access to the session state is not enough and variables should also be accessible: text_area for example does not update the session state before your next click outside of the element, which means that if the downloaded file depends on the text_area value you need to take it from the local variable it is assigned to and not it's session state.

We are shipping dynamic expanders in the 1.55 release targeted for this week! This feature should solve the issue here because it allows programmatic control of the expander via session state. Let me know if you have any feedback!

## UPdate

This will be available in 1.64+ via the `live` parameter on `st.text_input` ([#16662](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16662)). `live=True` commits the value after a 250ms pause while typing (or pass a duration like `"300ms"`). Prefer wrapping the live UI in a fragment so typing doesn't rerun the rest of the app:

```python
@st.fragment
def search():
    query = st.text_input("Search", type="search", live=True)
    st.write("You searched for:", query)

search()
```
